problems.title: Exergy of a heat supply
problems.scenario:
**2000 kJ** of heat is supplied from a reservoir at **800 K**. The environment is at $T_0 = 300\ \text{K}$.

Find the **exergy** of this heat, in kJ.
hints: Heat carries only the Carnot fraction of its energy as exergy.
$X = (1 - T_0/T)Q$, temperatures in K.
problems.solution:
Only the Carnot-weighted part of the heat is work potential:

$$X = \left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T}\right)Q = \left(1 - \frac{300}{800}\right)(2000) = 0.625 \times 2000 = 1250\ \text{kJ}$$

The other 750 kJ is energy that cannot be converted to work even by an ideal device.

problems.title: Exergy destruction from entropy generation
problems.scenario:
A process generates **0.80 kJ/K** of entropy. The environment is at $T_0 = 295\ \text{K}$.

Find the **exergy destroyed**, in kJ.
hints: Use the Gouy–Stodola relation.
$X_{dest} = T_0\, S_{gen}$.
problems.solution:
$$X_{dest} = T_0\, S_{gen} = 295 \times 0.80 = 236\ \text{kJ}$$

Every unit of generated entropy costs $T_0$ worth of lost work potential.

problems.title: Flow-exergy drop across a device
problems.scenario:
Steam enters a device at $h_1 = 3000\ \text{kJ/kg}$, $s_1 = 6.5\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$ and leaves at $h_2 = 2700\ \text{kJ/kg}$, $s_2 = 6.8\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$. The environment is at $T_0 = 300\ \text{K}$.

Find the **decrease in flow exergy**, $\psi_1 - \psi_2$, in kJ/kg.
hints: Neglecting KE/PE, $\psi = (h - h_0) - T_0(s - s_0)$, so the dead-state terms cancel in the difference.
problems.solution:
The dead-state reference cancels when you take the difference:

$$\psi_1 - \psi_2 = (h_1 - h_2) - T_0(s_1 - s_2) = (3000 - 2700) - 300(6.5 - 6.8)$$

$$= 300 - 300(-0.3) = 300 + 90 = 390\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

The entropy *rise* (irreversibility) adds to the available work drop here.

problems.title: Reversible work of a turbine
problems.scenario:
A turbine's inlet stream has a flow exergy of **900 kJ/kg** and its exit stream **300 kJ/kg**.

Find the **reversible work** output per unit mass, in kJ/kg.
hints: The reversible work equals the drop in flow exergy across the device.
$w_{rev} = \psi_1 - \psi_2$.
problems.solution:
The maximum (reversible) work is the exergy the stream gives up:

$$w_{rev} = \psi_1 - \psi_2 = 900 - 300 = 600\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

Any real turbine produces less than this; the shortfall is the destroyed exergy. (If the actual work were, say, 480 kJ/kg, then $\eta_{II} = 480/600 = 0.80$.)

problems.title: Exergy destroyed by heat conduction
problems.scenario:
Heat flows steadily at **10 kW** through a wall from a hot side at **600 K** to the surroundings at **300 K** ($T_0 = 300\ \text{K}$).

Find the **rate of exergy destruction**, in kW.
hints: Exergy enters with the hot heat and leaves with the cold heat; the difference is destroyed.
$\dot X_{dest} = (1 - T_0/T_H)\dot Q - (1 - T_0/T_L)\dot Q$. With $T_L = T_0$ the exit exergy is zero.
problems.solution:
Exergy carried in by the heat at 600 K, minus exergy carried out at 300 K:

$$\dot X_{dest} = \left(1 - \frac{300}{600}\right)(10) - \left(1 - \frac{300}{300}\right)(10) = 0.5(10) - 0 = 5\ \text{kW}$$

Conducting heat across a 300 K gap throws away half its work potential — exergy analysis exposes what an energy balance (which sees 10 kW in = 10 kW out) completely misses.

problems.title: Exergy of a hot iron block
problems.scenario:
A **50 kg** iron block ($c = 0.45\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$) is at **500 K** in an environment at $T_0 = 300\ \text{K}$.

Find the **exergy** of the block (the maximum work extractable as it cools to the dead state), in kJ.
hints: For an incompressible solid the volume term vanishes; exergy comes from the temperature difference.
$X = m\left[c(T - T_0) - T_0\,c\ln(T/T_0)\right]$.
The first term is the energy; the second subtracts the unavailable part.
problems.solution:
For an incompressible substance the exergy is the energy above the dead state minus the unavailable ($T_0\Delta s$) part:

$$X = m\left[c(T - T_0) - T_0\,c\ln\frac{T}{T_0}\right]$$

$$= 50\left[0.45(500 - 300) - 300(0.45)\ln\frac{500}{300}\right]$$

$$= 50\left[90 - 135 \times 0.5108\right] = 50\,[90 - 68.96] = 50 \times 21.04 = 1052\ \text{kJ}$$

Though the block holds $mc\,\Delta T = 4500$ kJ of energy above ambient, only ~1052 kJ of it is *useful work* — the rest is unavailable.

problems.title: Turbine exergy destruction & second-law efficiency
problems.scenario:
Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at $h_1 = 3200\ \text{kJ/kg}$, $s_1 = 6.8\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$ and leaves at $h_2 = 2600\ \text{kJ/kg}$, $s_2 = 7.1\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$. The actual work output is **560 kJ/kg** and $T_0 = 295\ \text{K}$.

Find the **exergy destroyed** per unit mass, in kJ/kg.
hints: First find the reversible work = drop in flow exergy $\psi_1 - \psi_2 = (h_1-h_2) - T_0(s_1-s_2)$.
Exergy destroyed = reversible work − actual work.
$x_{dest} = (\psi_1 - \psi_2) - w_{actual}$.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — reversible work** (flow-exergy drop):

$$\psi_1 - \psi_2 = (h_1 - h_2) - T_0(s_1 - s_2) = (3200 - 2600) - 295(6.8 - 7.1)$$

$$= 600 - 295(-0.3) = 600 + 88.5 = 688.5\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

**Step 2 — destroyed exergy** is the gap between reversible and actual work:

$$x_{dest} = (\psi_1 - \psi_2) - w_{actual} = 688.5 - 560 = 128.5\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

(Equivalently $\eta_{II} = 560/688.5 = 0.81$.)

problems.title: Exergy destroyed by mixing water
problems.scenario:
**2 kg** of water at **360 K** is mixed with **3 kg** of water at **300 K** in an insulated container ($c = 4.18\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$, $T_0 = 300\ \text{K}$).

Find the **exergy destroyed** by the mixing, in kJ.
hints: Three steps: equilibrium temperature (energy balance), then $S_{gen}$, then $X_{dest} = T_0 S_{gen}$.
$S_{gen} = m_1 c\ln(T_{eq}/T_1) + m_2 c\ln(T_{eq}/T_2)$.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — equilibrium temperature** (insulated, equal $c$):

$$T_{eq} = \frac{2(360) + 3(300)}{5} = \frac{1620}{5} = 324\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — entropy generated:**

$$S_{gen} = 2(4.18)\ln\frac{324}{360} + 3(4.18)\ln\frac{324}{300} = 8.36(-0.1054) + 12.54(0.0770) = 0.0843\ \text{kJ/K}$$

**Step 3 — exergy destroyed:**

$$X_{dest} = T_0\,S_{gen} = 300 \times 0.0843 = 25.3\ \text{kJ}$$

Mixing two streams at different temperatures is irreversible, so it quietly destroys ~25 kJ of work potential.

problems.title: Irreversibility of an actual heat engine
problems.scenario:
A heat engine receives heat from a source at **1100 K** at a rate of **400 kW**, and rejects waste heat to a medium at **320 K**. Its measured (actual) power output is **120 kW**. The environment is at $T_0 = 298\ \text{K}$.

Find the **rate of irreversibility** (the wasted work potential), in kW.
hints: The 'reversible power' uses the Carnot efficiency between the *actual* source and sink temperatures — **not** $T_0$. $T_0$ only matters if the sink happens to be the environment itself.
$\dot W_{rev} = \eta_{th,rev}\,\dot Q_H$, with $\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - T_L/T_H$ using $T_H=1100\ \text{K}$, $T_L=320\ \text{K}$.
Irreversibility is simply the gap between the best-possible and the actual: $\dot I = \dot W_{rev} - \dot W_{act}$.
problems.solution:
**Reversible (best-possible) power**, using the *actual* reservoir temperatures (1100 K and 320 K — not the dead-state $T_0$, which plays no role here since neither reservoir *is* the environment):

$$\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{320}{1100} = 0.7091$$

$$\dot W_{rev} = \eta_{th,rev}\,\dot Q_H = 0.7091\times400 = 283.6\ \text{kW}$$

**Irreversibility** — the gap between what's ideally possible and what's actually delivered:

$$\dot I = \dot W_{rev} - \dot W_{act} = 283.6 - 120 = 163.6\ \text{kW} \approx 164\ \text{kW}$$

(As a bonus, the second-law efficiency is $\eta_{II} = \dot W_{act}/\dot W_{rev} = 120/283.6 = 0.423$.) A common mistake is using $T_0$ in place of $T_L$ in the Carnot efficiency here — but $T_0$ only enters when the *environment itself* is one of the reservoirs.

problems.title: Why resistance heating wastes exergy
problems.scenario:
A house loses heat at **35,000 kJ/h** when the outside temperature is **4°C**. It is heated by **electric resistance heaters** and kept at **25°C**.

Find the **reversible (minimum possible) work input** for this heating, in kW. *(The actual electrical input, by contrast, equals the full heat demand — a resistance heater has no 'COP' advantage.)*
hints: The heat *demand* rate is $\dot Q_H = 35{,}000/3600$ kW — this is what the resistance heater actually consumes (its 'COP' is effectively 1).
The *minimum* work to deliver this heat would come from a reversible (Carnot) heat pump between the house (298 K) and outdoors (277 K): $COP_{rev} = T_H/(T_H-T_L)$.
$\dot W_{rev} = \dot Q_H/COP_{rev}$.
problems.solution:
**Heat demand rate** (this is exactly what the resistance heater draws as electricity, since it converts electricity to heat 1-for-1):

$$\dot Q_H = \frac{35{,}000}{3600} = 9.722\ \text{kW}$$

**Best possible way to deliver it** — a reversible heat pump between the house (298 K) and outdoor air (277 K):

$$COP_{rev} = \frac{T_H}{T_H-T_L} = \frac{298.15}{298.15-277.15} = 14.20$$

$$\dot W_{rev} = \frac{\dot Q_H}{COP_{rev}} = \frac{9.722}{14.20} = 0.685\ \text{kW}$$

The resistance heater needs the full **9.72 kW**, while a reversible heat pump could deliver the same warmth for just **0.685 kW** — the other **9.04 kW** is pure waste (the irreversibility), even though *both* methods satisfy the first law perfectly. This is exactly why heat pumps beat resistance heating.
